sections.h: The king under the covenant (1 Samuel 12–13)
sections.b: At Gilgal Samuel accepts the new king but sets him under the same covenant as the people: if both fear the LORD and listen to his voice, all will be well; if not, "you and your king alike will be swept away" (1 Samuel 12:25). Saul's first test comes quickly. He offers the burnt offering at Gilgal instead of waiting for Samuel, and Samuel tells him his kingship will not last, because the LORD has searched for "a man to suit his own heart" (1 Samuel 13:14). In Israel the king is not above God's word as spoken by the prophet.

Saul's second failure, sparing Agag and the best of Amalek's animals, brings final rejection: "You rejected the LORD's word, so he has rejected you as king" (1 Samuel 15:23). The robe that tears in Samuel's hand becomes a sign that the kingdom is torn away and given to "a neighbor of yours who is better than you" (1 Samuel 15:28). The rest of 1 Samuel shows Saul holding a throne God has already given to another.

common: Saul's failure shows that Israel's king had to obey the prophetic word, not act on his own judgment.
Many modern literary readers (Gunn, Exum) read Saul as a tragic figure, more sinned against than the narrative's verdict admits.

sections.b: Samuel hands leadership to Saul with a speech at Gilgal. He asks the people to testify whether he ever took an ox or a donkey or a bribe, and they clear him. He reviews Israel's history and calls down thunder in the dry season as a sign. He promises never to stop praying for the people. Samuel does not retire: he remains the prophet who speaks God's word to the king.

sections.h: The prophet who rejects and anoints (1 Samuel 13–16)
sections.b: Twice Samuel announces Saul's rejection (1 Samuel 13:13–14; 1 Samuel 15:22–29). He cries out all night when the LORD regrets making Saul king, and he grieves over Saul until God sends him to Bethlehem. There he anoints David, nearly choosing the tall Eliab first. Samuel then withdraws to Ramah, where David later flees to him and Saul's messengers are overcome by the Spirit (1 Samuel 19:18–24).

Saul fails twice. At Gilgal he offers the sacrifice rather than wait for Samuel (1 Samuel 13); against Amalek he spares the king and the best animals (1 Samuel 15). Each time he explains himself: the people were leaving, the animals were for sacrifice, he was afraid of the people. Each time Samuel answers that the LORD wants obedience. Saul confesses, "I have sinned," but seems more concerned to be honored before the elders (1 Samuel 15:30).

Saul forbids his army to eat until evening, and Jonathan, not knowing, tastes honey. When the lot falls on Jonathan, Saul is ready to kill him, but the people ransom him. The scene shows Saul's habit of grand religious gestures that harm his own people.

sections.h: Jealousy and the evil spirit (1 Samuel 16–20)
sections.b: As the LORD's Spirit leaves Saul, an evil spirit from the LORD troubles him. David's music relieves him, but after Goliath's defeat the women's song turns Saul against David. He throws his spear at David twice and at Jonathan once, plots to have the Philistines kill David, and sends men to his house. He calls him only "the son of Jesse." When Saul goes after David at Ramah, the Spirit overwhelms him, and people ask, "Is Saul also among the prophets?"

common: Saul is a tragic figure whose fear and jealousy led him to fight against God's chosen successor.
uncommon: Some readers diagnose Saul with a mental illness, such as depression or paranoia, described in the language of an evil spirit.

sections.b: Jonathan opens the war with the Philistines by striking their post at Geba (1 Samuel 13:3). Then, with only his armor-bearer, he climbs between the crags Bozez and Seneh to attack a Philistine post, saying the LORD can save with many or with few (1 Samuel 14:6). A panic from God follows. Unaware of his father's oath, he eats honey and is nearly put to death, until the people ransom him.

After Goliath's defeat, "Jonathan's life was tied up with David's life" (1 Samuel 18:1). He makes a covenant with David and gives him his robe and weapons. He speaks for David to his father, warns him of danger, and finally learns, when Saul's spear flies at him, that his father means to kill David. Jonathan asks David for loyal love to his family forever, and the two part in tears with an oath that binds their offspring.

common: Jonathan is the Bible's great model of loyal, self-giving friendship.
uncommon: Some modern scholars read the bond between Jonathan and David as romantic or erotic; others argue it is covenant loyalty expressed in political language.

sections.b: David is the youngest of Jesse's eight sons, out with the sheep when Samuel comes. The LORD rejects his tall brother Eliab, saying he looks at the heart, and David is anointed "among his brothers." The Spirit of the LORD sweeps down on him from that day. He enters Saul's service as a musician and armor-bearer, described as a skilled player, a strong fighter, good with words, handsome, and "the LORD is with him" (1 Samuel 16:18).

David kills Goliath in the name of the LORD of Armies, wins every battle, and is loved by all Israel and Judah. He marries Saul's daughter Michal after paying a bride-price of Philistine foreskins. But Saul's jealousy grows. David escapes the spear twice, flees through a window, takes refuge with Samuel at Ramah, and parts from Jonathan to begin his life as a fugitive.

The Philistines and Israel face each other across the Valley of Elah. Goliath of Gath, in bronze armor with a spear like a weaver's beam, challenges Israel to single combat for forty days. David, bringing food to his brothers, hears the challenge and volunteers. He refuses Saul's armor and goes out with a shepherd's stick, a sling and five stones, declaring that "The battle belongs to the LORD" (1 Samuel 17:47). His stone strikes Goliath in the forehead, and he cuts off the giant's head with his own sword.

The oldest Greek text lacks about 44 percent of chapters 17–18 (39 of 88 verses), giving a shorter, smoother story. Scholars debate whether the Greek preserves an earlier version (Tov, Lust, and more recent scholars such as Auld and Ho) or shortened the long Hebrew (Barthélemy, Gooding); the question is open. Goliath's height differs: four cubits and a span in 4QSam-a, the Old Greek and Josephus, which this site follows, and six cubits and a span in the Masoretic Text. And 2 Samuel 21:19 says Elhanan killed Goliath, while 1 Chronicles 20:5 says Elhanan killed Goliath's brother.

Michal is Saul's younger daughter (1 Samuel 14:49). She is the only woman in Hebrew narrative said to love a man. Saul uses her love as bait, asking for a hundred Philistine foreskins as the bride-price in the hope that David will die. David brings the price, and they marry.

When Saul sends men to kill David, Michal lowers him through a window, puts the household god in his bed covered with goat hair, and tells the messengers he is sick. Confronted by her father, she claims David threatened her. Like Rachel, she deceives her father with household gods. She will soon be given to another man (1 Samuel 25:44).

1 Samuel 15 is the classic text for the question of divine regret. The LORD says, "I regret making Saul king" (1 Samuel 15:11), and the chapter ends: "the LORD regretted having made Saul king over Israel" (1 Samuel 15:35). But between them Samuel says, "Israel's Enduring One does not lie and does not regret. He is not a human being, to have regrets" (1 Samuel 15:29). The same Hebrew verb, nacham, is used in all three verses.

Interpreters resolve this in different ways. Many say 15:29 refers to God's decision to reject Saul, which he will not reverse, while 15:11 and 15:35 describe God's grief over Saul's failure. Classical theologians read "regret" as language suited to human understanding (Calvin, Institutes 1.17.12–14). Others take the tension at face value as part of the Bible's way of speaking about a God who is both faithful and personally involved.

When the LORD's Spirit turns away from Saul, "an evil spirit from the LORD kept terrifying him" (1 Samuel 16:14). David is brought to play the lyre, and the spirit leaves Saul for a time. Later the spirit comes on Saul as David plays, and Saul throws the spear (1 Samuel 18:10–11; 1 Samuel 19:9–10). The spirit "sweeps down" on Saul with the same verb used when the Spirit of God empowered him (1 Samuel 10:6; 1 Samuel 11:6).

Saul's servants suggest that a skilled lyre player could relieve the king's torment. David is chosen, and whenever the spirit troubles Saul, David plays and Saul can breathe again (1 Samuel 16:23). This is one of the earliest descriptions of music as therapy. David is remembered as "the sweet singer of Israel" (2 Samuel 23:1, though the phrase may mean "the favorite of Israel's songs"), and many psalms bear his name.

Women come out with tambourines and lutes to greet the returning army, singing, "Saul has struck his thousands, / David his tens of thousands" (1 Samuel 18:7). The custom recalls Miriam's song and Jephthah's daughter. The song, praising both men, provokes Saul's jealousy.

Samuel fills his horn with oil and anoints Jesse's youngest son "among his brothers" (1 Samuel 16:13). From that day the Spirit of the LORD sweeps down on David. The anointing is private; David will be anointed again publicly as king of Judah (2 Samuel 2:4) and of Israel (2 Samuel 5:3). The link between anointing and the Spirit runs through to Isaiah 61:1 and Jesus' baptism.

The Greek and Latin text of 1 Samuel 14:41 is the only biblical passage showing how the Urim and Thummim may have been used: Saul asks that Urim come out if the guilt lies with him or Jonathan, Thummim if it lies with the people. The Hebrew text is shorter, probably from a scribal skip. Most modern translations follow the longer text. The result singles out Jonathan.

sections.h: Jonathan taken by the lot (1 Samuel 14)
sections.b: When God does not answer Saul, he concludes someone has sinned and casts lots, first between the people and Saul's family, then between Saul and Jonathan. The lot falls on Jonathan, who had eaten honey without knowing of the oath. The process recalls the discovery of Achan (Joshua 7:14–18), but the outcome differs: the people refuse to let Jonathan die.

Samuel orders Saul to put Amalek under the ban, killing all people and animals, because of Amalek's attack on Israel in the wilderness. Saul spares the king and the best livestock, and is rejected for disobedience. The command troubled ancient readers too: the Talmud has Saul protest that the children and animals had done nothing, and a heavenly voice answer, "Do not be righteous too much" (Yoma 22b; Ecclesiastes 7:16). Maimonides rules that peace must be offered first even to Amalek (Laws of Kings 6:1–4). Modern interpreters differ: a unique judgment (traditional readers), ancient war hyperbole (Copan and Flannagan, Younger), or a stage in Israel's understanding that later revelation corrects (Seibert).

sections.h: "The battle belongs to the LORD" (1 Samuel 17)
sections.b: David's words to Goliath sum up the theology of holy war: the LORD saves, and not by sword and spear (1 Samuel 17:47). The same conviction drives Jonathan's attack at Michmash (1 Samuel 14:6). Both stories show victory coming through faith and a panic sent by God, not by numbers or weapons.

The LORD commands Saul to destroy Amalek to punish what it did to Israel on the way up from Egypt. Saul defeats them from Havilah to Shur but spares King Agag and the best animals. Samuel kills Agag at Gilgal. Amalekites appear again later in David's story (1 Samuel 30), and Jewish tradition links Agag to Haman "the Agagite" in Esther.

In Saul's day the Philistines hold posts deep in Israel's hill country. They keep Israel from having smiths, so Israelites must go to them to sharpen tools, and only Saul and Jonathan have swords (1 Samuel 13:19–22). They field chariots and send out raiding parties. Their champion Goliath of Gath, with armor like an Aegean warrior's, challenges Israel to single combat. Archaeology at Gath (Tell es-Safi) and Ekron shows wealthy, Aegean-influenced cities.

Goliath comes from Gath, one of the cities where the Anakim survived (Joshua 11:22). His height is four cubits and a span in 4QSam-a, the Old Greek and Josephus, about six feet nine inches, which this site follows; the Masoretic Text has six cubits and a span, nearly ten feet. 2 Samuel 21:15–22 lists other giants of Gath, "born to the Rapha," killed by David's men.

At Naioth in Ramah a company of prophets prophesies with Samuel at their head. Saul's three groups of messengers, then Saul himself, are overcome by the Spirit and prophesy. Saul strips and lies on the ground all day and night. The scene shows ecstatic prophecy, known also from Mari and elsewhere in the ancient Near East, and repeats the proverb "Is Saul also among the prophets?" (1 Samuel 19:24).

sections.h: The Spirit moves from Saul to David (1 Samuel 16)
sections.b: When Samuel anoints David, "the LORD's Spirit swept down on David" (1 Samuel 16:13), and in the next verse the Spirit turns away from Saul. In the Old Testament the Spirit equips leaders for their task; here it marks the transfer of God's favor. David later prays, "Your holy spirit, do not take it from me" (Psalm 51:11), perhaps remembering Saul.
When Saul sends messengers to seize David at Ramah, the Spirit of God comes on them and they prophesy. The Spirit then overwhelms Saul himself. The Spirit acts here as a shield for the anointed one.

In 1 Samuel "the LORD's anointed" (meshiach YHWH) is the king. Samuel calls Saul the LORD's anointed in his farewell speech (1 Samuel 12:3; 1 Samuel 12:5), and when he sees Eliab he says, "Surely the LORD's anointed stands here before him" (1 Samuel 16:6). David is anointed with oil at Bethlehem. Later David will refuse to harm Saul because he is the LORD's anointed (1 Samuel 24:6). From this royal title comes the hope for an anointed son of David, the Messiah.

sections.b: 1 Samuel is one of the books where the Greek translation and the Dead Sea Scrolls (especially 4QSam-a) differ most from the Masoretic Text. The best-known case is David and Goliath: the Old Greek lacks about 44 percent of chapters 17–18. Scholars disagree whether it preserves an earlier, shorter story or abbreviates the long one. 1 Samuel 13:1 has lost its numbers, 14:41 has probably lost a long phrase, and Goliath's height differs between witnesses.

sections.b: The bond between David and Jonathan (1 Samuel 18:1–4; 1 Samuel 20:17; 1 Samuel 20:41; 2 Samuel 1:26) is often discussed in debates over same-sex relationships. Tom Horner and Susan Ackerman read it as romantic or erotic, citing Jonathan's "delight" in David (1 Samuel 19:1; compare Genesis 34:19), Saul's taunt about "nakedness" (1 Samuel 20:30), the kisses of 1 Samuel 20:41 and David's lament that Jonathan's love surpassed the love of women. Saul Olyan studies the same words as covenant language between partners, without drawing conclusions for the modern moral debate. Robert Gagnon argues that nothing in the text suggests a sexual relationship, that kissing and weeping were normal between male friends, and that the Bible's sexual vocabulary is absent. Most commentators read covenant friendship; a substantial minority sees homoerotic overtones.

Gilgal, Israel's first camp in the land, is the setting for Saul's renewal as king, Samuel's farewell (perhaps), Saul's unlawful sacrifice (1 Samuel 13:8–14), and his final rejection and Agag's execution (1 Samuel 15:12–33). The place of Israel's beginning becomes the place of Saul's end.

Gibeah of Saul is Saul's home and capital (1 Samuel 15:34). Saul sits there under a pomegranate tree (1 Samuel 14:2) and holds his new-moon feast there (1 Samuel 20). Jonathan's force is stationed there before the battle of Michmash.

Samuel comes to Bethlehem to anoint one of Jesse's sons (1 Samuel 16:1–13). David is "the son of that Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judah" (1 Samuel 17:12) and gives his family's yearly sacrifice there as his excuse to miss Saul's feast (1 Samuel 20:6). From here comes the expectation that a ruler will come from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2).

Michal puts the household god in David's bed to fool Saul's men (1 Samuel 19:13–16). The image must have been human-sized. Shortly before, Samuel had compared stubbornness to the evil of household gods (1 Samuel 15:23). The scene parallels Rachel hiding Laban's household gods (Genesis 31:34–35).

Jonathan makes a covenant with David because he loves him (1 Samuel 18:3), and later makes it with "David's house" (1 Samuel 20:16). David calls it "a covenant of the LORD" (1 Samuel 20:8). It binds both men and their offspring "for all time" (1 Samuel 20:42). David later keeps it by caring for Jonathan's son Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9; 2 Samuel 21:7).

sections.b: David asks Jonathan to deal with him in loyal love, because of their covenant (1 Samuel 20:8). Jonathan in turn asks David to show him "the LORD's loyal love" and never cut it off from his family (1 Samuel 20:14–15). Hesed here is the loyalty owed within a covenant, extended beyond death. Earlier Saul spared the Kenites because they showed Israel loyal love in the wilderness (1 Samuel 15:6).

When the people beg Samuel to pray for them, he promises never to sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for them (1 Samuel 12:19–23). When the LORD regrets making Saul king, Samuel cries out all night (1 Samuel 15:11). Jeremiah later names Moses and Samuel as Israel's great intercessors (Jeremiah 15:1).

Samuel's poem in 1 Samuel 15:22–23 sets obedience above sacrifice: "listening is better than sacrifice." The same idea appears in Hosea 6:6, Micah 6:6–8 and Psalm 51:16–17. Saul's unlawful burnt offering at Gilgal (1 Samuel 13:9) and his excuse that the spoil was for sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:15; 1 Samuel 15:21) show sacrifice used without obedience.
sections.refs: 1 Samuel 13:9–12; 1 Samuel 15:15; 1 Samuel 15:21–23; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6–8; Psalm 51:16–17

sections.b: Saul's oath that no one eats until evening nearly costs Jonathan his life (1 Samuel 14:24–45). His later oath that David will not be killed is broken almost at once (1 Samuel 19:6–10). Jonathan, by contrast, keeps his oaths to David (1 Samuel 20:12–17).

After the battle, starving soldiers kill animals on the ground and eat the meat with its blood (1 Samuel 14:32). The law forbids it (Leviticus 17:10–14). Saul has a stone rolled over so animals can be slaughtered and drained properly, building his first altar. Jonathan later warns his father against shedding innocent blood (1 Samuel 19:5).

Seven sons of Jesse pass before Samuel and are not chosen. The LORD rejects the tall Eliab, for "the LORD sees the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). The youngest, out with the sheep, is anointed. The pattern of the younger chosen over the elder runs from Abel and Isaac to Jacob, Joseph and Ephraim.

sections.h: The new moon at Saul's table (1 Samuel 20)
sections.b: The first day of the month was a feast day with sacrifices (Numbers 28:11–15). Saul holds a meal for his household, and David's absence is noticed. Saul thinks David must be ritually unclean on the first day, but on the second he is enraged. Jewish practice reads 1 Samuel 20:18–42 when a Sabbath falls just before the new moon.
